query: For steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to corrosion? Specify a controlled study capable of revealing the governing cause, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting evidence from prior findings, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Inducing compressive residual stresses via controlled mechanical surface treatments (such as UNSM) improves corrosion resistance in steels by enhancing grain boundary diffusion and promoting a more uniform and robust passive film.
generation.material_initial_state: Standard steel used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications with typical microstructure and baseline residual stress levels.
generation.intervention: Application of ultrasonic nanocrystal surface modification (UNSM) at optimized static load parameters to introduce controlled compressive residual stress.
generation.conditions: Testing under corrosive conditions representative of chemical-processing and nuclear environments (e.g., elevated temperature, high pressure, and aggressive chemical exposure) while varying the static load during UNSM treatment.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced grain boundary and surface diffusion that restructures the surface microstructure to form a continuous and stable passive film.
generation.mechanism: At a critical static load, the UNSM treatment increases grain boundary diffusion, which refines the surface microstructure and facilitates the formation and reinforcement of a passive film. This film acts as a barrier to corrosive agents. Loads exceeding the critical threshold may damage the microstructure, diminishing the protective effect.
generation.predicted_outcome: Steels treated with UNSM at optimal static loads will display lower corrosion rates, higher AC impedance, and improved passivation compared to untreated steels. Treatments above the critical load will result in degraded corrosion resistance relative to optimally treated samples.
generation.baseline: Untreated steel specimens exposed to identical corrosive environments, showing standard corrosion rates and passive film quality.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold for steels with similar compositions used in chemical-processing and nuclear power applications under the specific mechanical treatment and environmental conditions specified. Its validity for other steel types or under radically different environmental conditions is uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: The precise critical static load and its dependence on various steel compositions remain to be determined. Extrapolation to all steels in these industries requires further validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare multiple steel samples and apply UNSM treatment at three levels: below, at, and above the hypothesized critical static load. Expose all samples to a controlled corrosive environment reflective of chemical-processing and nuclear applications.
measurements: AC impedance spectroscopy to evaluate the integrity of the passive film
Cyclic polarization tests to measure corrosion rates
Microscopic analyses (SEM, EBSD) to assess changes in grain boundary diffusion and surface microstructure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If steel samples treated at the optimized (critical) static load do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in corrosion resistance (i.e., increased impedance, reduced corrosion rates) over untreated samples, or if samples treated with loads above the critical value do not show a decrease in corrosion resistance, then the proposed mechanism is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
## Abstract
To suppress stress corrosion-cracking, compressive residual stresses, such as shot peening, laser peening, water jet peening, ultrasonic peening, and ultrasonic nanocrystal surface modification (UNSM) are utilized. However, among the numerous techniques, there is little research about the corrosion effect of detailed conditions, such as static load or amplitude in UNSM. A study on UNSM among various techniques of adding compressive residual stress to Alloy 600 was conducted. The focus of this study was on the effect of the static load in UNSM on the corrosion properties of Alloy 600. Microstructure analysis was conducted using an optical microscope (OM), a scanning electron microscope (SEM), and electron backscattering diffraction (EBSD), while compressive residual stress was measured using a nano-indentation technique. A cyclic polarization test and the AC (Alternating Current)-impedance measurement were both used to analyze the corrosion properties. An increase in static load under critical static load enhanced the grain boundary diffusion, consequently strengthened the passive film, and facilitated the surface diffusion, thereby improving the passivation of Alloy 600
